title: Shaking After Drinking: Hangover Shakes vs. Withdrawal Tremors
excerpt: Why your hands shake after drinking, how to get rid of hangover shakes, how to tell them apart from alcohol withdrawal tremors, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Why your hands shake after drinking, how to stop hangover shakes, how to tell them from alcohol withdrawal tremors, and when shaking needs a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** shaky hands the morning after a night of drinking are common, and for most social drinkers they're a normal part of a hangover that fades within a day. They come from your nervous system rebounding after alcohol wears off, often made worse by low blood sugar, poor sleep, dehydration, and too much coffee. The fix is mostly food, fluids, rest, and time. But shaking after drinking can also be an early sign of alcohol withdrawal, which is a different and potentially dangerous condition. This guide explains how to tell the two apart, what actually helps, and when to get medical help.

**The quick rules:** Eat something with carbohydrates and protein, drink water, skip extra caffeine, and rest. Don't drink more alcohol to "steady your hands." If your shakes regularly go away only when you drink, if they come with heavy sweating, a racing heart, confusion, or seeing or hearing things that aren't there, or if you drink heavily most days, that points toward withdrawal, and you should talk to a doctor before cutting back on your own.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if** shaking comes with a seizure, confusion or disorientation, hallucinations (seeing, hearing, or feeling things that aren't there), a very high heart rate, chest pain, a high fever, or severe vomiting that stops you keeping fluids down. **See a doctor soon if** your hands shake most mornings, the shakes get better only after you drink, you've been drinking heavily for days or weeks and want to stop, the tremor lasts longer than a day or two, or you have diabetes and notice shakiness with sweating and confusion (a sign of low blood sugar). If you drink heavily every day, **do not stop suddenly without medical advice.** Alcohol withdrawal can be life-threatening, and doctors can make it much safer.

## Why You Get the Shakes After Drinking

Most people searching for "shaking after drinking" had a big night and woke up with trembling hands, a jittery feeling, and maybe a pounding heart. That combination has a few overlapping causes. Usually more than one is at work at once.

### 1. Your nervous system rebounds after alcohol wears off

Alcohol is a depressant. It slows your brain down in two main ways. It boosts the effect of **GABA**, the brain's main calming signal, and it dampens **glutamate**, one of the main excitatory signals, by blocking a type of receptor called NMDA.

Your brain doesn't like being pushed in one direction, so while you're drinking it starts adjusting to balance things out. When the alcohol leaves your blood the next morning, those adjustments are still in place, and for a while your nervous system runs a little too "hot." That rebound overexcitement can show up as a fine tremor in your hands, jumpiness, sensitivity to light and noise, and a vague sense of anxiety.

In an occasional drinker this rebound is small and short-lived. In someone who drinks heavily every day, the brain's adjustments are much bigger and longer-lasting, and the rebound is what we call alcohol withdrawal. It's the same basic process at a very different scale, which is why the difference matters so much (more on that below).

### 2. Low blood sugar

While your liver is busy breaking down alcohol, it's less able to make new glucose (a process called gluconeogenesis). If you drank on an empty stomach, skipped dinner, or haven't eaten since, your blood sugar can drift lower than usual by morning. Low blood sugar triggers a release of adrenaline, and adrenaline causes shakiness, sweating, a fast heartbeat, hunger, and irritability.

For most healthy people the dip is modest. It can be much more serious for people with diabetes, especially those who use insulin or certain diabetes pills, because alcohol can cause genuinely dangerous lows hours after drinking. If that applies to you, see our guide to [alcohol and blood sugar management](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025).

### 3. Stress hormones and a revved-up heart

A hangover is a stress state. Your body's "fight or flight" system (the sympathetic nervous system) tends to be more active the morning after heavy drinking, and stress hormones like adrenaline and cortisol are part of that picture. That's why shaky hands often arrive together with a racing pulse, sweating, and a jittery, on-edge feeling that many people call "hangxiety." Our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) covers the anxious side of that in more detail.

### 4. Poor sleep

Alcohol can help you fall asleep faster, but it breaks up sleep in the second half of the night as your body clears it. You get less REM sleep and more waking up. Even one bad night makes many people feel shaky, wired, and unsteady the next day, and it adds to everything else here. If you want the detail, see our article on [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025).

### 5. Dehydration and electrolytes

Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin, which normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. The result is more trips to the bathroom and some fluid loss. Being low on fluids can leave you lightheaded, weak, and a bit shaky, especially if you also sweated, vomited, or had diarrhea.

It's worth being honest here: dehydration gets more credit for hangovers than the evidence supports. Studies that measured electrolytes in hungover people haven't found a strong link between those levels and how bad the hangover felt. Fluids help you feel better, but they're one piece of the puzzle rather than the main cause of the shakes. If you've been sick, an electrolyte drink makes more sense than plain water. Our guide to [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers when they're worth it.

### 6. Too much caffeine (and other stimulants)

Coffee is the default hangover move, and a cup is fine. But caffeine on top of an already overactive nervous system, low blood sugar, and an empty stomach is a reliable way to make your hands shake more. Energy drinks, pre-workout powders, and nicotine can do the same. Any stimulant drugs used the night before can also cause tremor and jitteriness the next day, and mixing them with alcohol carries its own serious risks.

## Hangover Shakes vs. Withdrawal Tremors: How to Tell the Difference

This is the most important section on the page. A hangover tremor and an alcohol withdrawal tremor can feel similar in the moment, but they mean very different things.

| | Hangover shakes | Withdrawal tremor |
|---|---|---|
| **Who gets it** | Anyone after a heavy night, including occasional drinkers | Usually people who have been drinking heavily most days for weeks or longer |
| **Timing** | The morning after a big night, as blood alcohol returns to zero | Often begins roughly 6 to 24 hours after the last drink, and can build over the next day or two |
| **How long it lasts** | Usually fades within a day as the hangover clears | Can last several days and may get worse before it gets better |
| **What helps** | Food, fluids, rest, time | Often eased by drinking again, which is a warning sign rather than a fix |
| **Other symptoms** | Headache, tiredness, nausea, thirst, mild anxiety | Heavy sweating, fast heartbeat, high blood pressure, strong anxiety or agitation, trouble sleeping, nausea or vomiting |
| **Danger signs** | Rare | Can progress to seizures, hallucinations, or delirium tremens (DTs), a medical emergency |

### Three questions to ask yourself

1. **Do I drink heavily most days, or have I been on a long run of heavy drinking?** A tremor after one big Saturday is very different from a tremor after three weeks of drinking every night.
2. **Does a drink make the shaking go away?** If alcohol reliably settles your hands, your body is likely depending on it. Needing a drink in the morning to steady your nerves (sometimes called an "eye-opener") is one of the classic screening questions doctors use for alcohol problems.
3. **Is this happening more often, or getting worse?** Shakes that used to be rare but now show up most mornings, or that start sooner after your last drink, are worth taking seriously.

If you answered yes to any of these, please read the next section before doing anything else.

## If Your Shakes Might Be Withdrawal: Read This First

This page is written for social drinkers dealing with a rough morning. But "shaking after drinking" is also one of the earliest signs of physical alcohol dependence, and it's important to say plainly what that means.

**Alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous.** In people who are physically dependent, stopping suddenly can lead to seizures and, in more severe cases, delirium tremens, which involves confusion, hallucinations, fever, and a racing heart. DTs typically appear a couple of days or more after the last drink and need hospital treatment. Seizures tend to happen earlier, within the first day or two. People who have been through withdrawal before can be at higher risk of worse symptoms next time.

**What to do:**

- **Don't stop cold turkey on your own if you drink heavily every day.** That advice surprises people, but it's standard medical guidance. A doctor can assess your risk and, if needed, prescribe medication (commonly a benzodiazepine) to make withdrawal safe. Many people can do this as outpatients. Others need a short supervised stay.
- **Don't treat it with more alcohol.** Drinking to stop the shakes delays withdrawal; it doesn't prevent it, and it deepens the cycle.
- **Don't rely on supplements, including DHM.** No supplement treats alcohol withdrawal or prevents withdrawal seizures.
- **Get emergency help** for a seizure, confusion, hallucinations, high fever, or a very fast heart rate. Call 911.

If you're in the US and want confidential help finding treatment, the SAMHSA National Helpline is free and open around the clock at **1-800-662-4357**. Your own doctor is also a good, judgment-free place to start. Talking about drinking is routine for them.

## How to Get Rid of the Shakes After Drinking

If you're confident this is an ordinary hangover tremor, here's what actually helps. None of it is a quick switch. The goal is to remove the things that make the shaking worse and let your nervous system settle.

### 1. Eat something, soon

This is the single most useful step, because it deals with low blood sugar directly. Aim for some easily digested carbohydrates plus a bit of protein. Good options:

- Toast, crackers, or a bagel with eggs or peanut butter
- Oatmeal with a banana
- A sandwich or a bowl of rice with something on top
- If your stomach is very unsettled, start small: a few crackers, a little juice, or some broth, then build up

A small glass of fruit juice or a sports drink gives you fast sugar if you feel weak and sweaty, but follow it with real food so you don't dip again. If you have diabetes, follow your own hypoglycemia plan and check your glucose.

### 2. Drink fluids steadily

Sip water through the morning rather than chugging a liter at once, which can upset an already queasy stomach. If you've vomited, had diarrhea, or sweated a lot, an oral rehydration drink or electrolyte mix helps replace salts as well as water.

### 3. Go easy on the caffeine

If you're a regular coffee drinker, a normal cup can stop a caffeine-withdrawal headache from piling on. Just don't use extra coffee or energy drinks to push through. If your hands are already shaking, more stimulant usually makes it worse.

### 4. Rest, and sleep if you can

A nap won't erase a hangover, but making up for broken sleep helps your nervous system calm down. Keep the room dark and cool, and put your phone down.

### 5. Calm your body down directly

Shaky hands and a racing heart feed anxiety, and anxiety feeds the shaking. Slow breathing helps break that loop. Try breathing in through your nose for about four seconds and out slowly for about six, for a few minutes. A short, easy walk outdoors can also help. Skip a hard workout; it raises your heart rate and stress hormones further. A warm shower can feel good. Avoid saunas when you're dehydrated.

### 6. Skip the "hair of the dog"

A drink in the morning may take the edge off the shakes for an hour or two, because you're temporarily topping up the alcohol your nervous system was adjusting to. It just postpones the rebound and adds to the overall load. And if you find a drink is the only thing that works, see the withdrawal section above.

### 7. Be careful with medications

There's no specific medicine for hangover shakes. Pain relievers treat headaches, not tremor, and each comes with its own alcohol cautions: acetaminophen is harder on the liver after heavy drinking, while ibuprofen and aspirin are harder on the stomach. Never take sedatives, sleeping pills, or someone else's anxiety medication to calm the shakes after drinking. Combining sedatives with alcohol still in your system can dangerously slow your breathing.

### 8. Give it time

Most hangover symptoms, including the shakes, ease within about 24 hours as your body finishes recovering. Our article on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) walks through the typical timeline and what can stretch it out. If your tremor is still there after a day or two of not drinking, see a doctor.

## What About Magnesium, B Vitamins, and Other Supplements?

You'll see a lot of supplement advice for hangover shakes online. Here's an honest view:

- **Magnesium.** Heavy drinking can lower magnesium levels over time, and low magnesium can contribute to muscle twitching and tremor. For an occasional big night, there's no good evidence that a magnesium supplement stops next-day shakes, but it's generally safe at normal doses for people with healthy kidneys. Our [magnesium for hangovers guide](/never-hungover/magnesium-hangover-hangxiety-glycinate-vs-citrate-2026) compares the forms.
- **B vitamins.** Long-term heavy drinking depletes thiamine (vitamin B1), and serious thiamine deficiency causes real neurological problems. That's why doctors give thiamine during alcohol withdrawal treatment. For a one-off hangover, there's no good evidence that B vitamins fix shaking.
- **Electrolyte mixes.** Useful if you've lost fluid through vomiting, diarrhea, or sweating. Less important otherwise.
- **Herbal "calming" products.** Some contain sedating ingredients that don't mix well with alcohol still in your system. Read labels and check with a pharmacist if you take other medications.

No supplement treats or prevents alcohol withdrawal. If your shakes might be withdrawal, see a doctor rather than shopping for a pill.

## Could It Be Something Other Than Alcohol?

Sometimes the shaking after drinking isn't really about the alcohol, or not only about it. A few other causes are worth knowing:

- **Essential tremor.** This is a common, usually harmless condition that causes shaking hands, often worse when you're holding something or reaching. Many people with essential tremor notice that a drink temporarily calms their tremor, and then it comes back, sometimes more noticeably, as the alcohol wears off. If you have a tremor even on days you haven't been drinking, it's worth getting checked.
- **Medications.** Some antidepressants, asthma inhalers, thyroid medication, lithium, ADHD stimulants, and decongestants can cause tremor on their own. A hangover can make that more noticeable.
- **An overactive thyroid.** This can cause shaky hands, a fast heart, sweating, and weight loss. A simple blood test can rule it out.
- **Anxiety.** Anxiety can cause trembling on its own, and alcohol tends to make anxiety worse the next day. Our guide to [alcohol and anxiety](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-anxiety-breaking-the-cycle-naturally-2025) explains that cycle.
- **Low blood sugar from other causes**, especially in people with diabetes.

If you notice a tremor that happens regardless of drinking, or one that's getting worse over time, mention it to your doctor.

## How to Avoid the Shakes Next Time

The shakes track closely with how much you drank and how you drank it. The habits that make a real difference:

- **Eat a proper meal before and while you drink.** Food slows alcohol absorption and helps keep your blood sugar steadier overnight.
- **Pace yourself.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though that varies a lot. Drinking faster than that is what builds up the overnight rebound.
- **Alternate with water.** It slows you down and limits fluid loss.
- **Have a snack before bed** if you've been drinking and haven't eaten much.
- **Go easy on caffeine and energy drinks**, both mixed into drinks and the morning after.
- **Protect your sleep.** Stop drinking a few hours before bed if you can.
- **Keep heavy nights occasional.** The more often you drink heavily, the bigger the rebound gets, and the closer you move toward the withdrawal end of the scale.

Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through the strategies with the best evidence behind them.

### Where DHM fits (and where it doesn't)

Some people add a supplement to their routine on nights out. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound that has attracted interest partly because of how it interacts with the same GABA-A receptors involved in the nervous-system rebound described above. Most of that research is in animals, including a well-known 2012 rodent study in the *Journal of Neuroscience* that found DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal in rats. Human evidence is limited, and there is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangover shakes in people. It certainly is not a treatment for alcohol withdrawal, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe.

If you're an occasional drinker and want to try DHM alongside the basics of food, water, and pacing, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when. If you take prescription medication, especially sedatives or anything for anxiety, sleep, or seizures, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- Shaky hands the morning after a heavy night are common and usually come from your nervous system rebounding after alcohol, made worse by low blood sugar, poor sleep, dehydration, and caffeine.
- The best fixes are simple: eat carbohydrates and protein, sip fluids, limit caffeine, rest, and give it time. Most hangover shakes fade within a day.
- Don't drink more to stop the shaking, and don't take sedatives with alcohol in your system.
- Shakes that come most mornings, ease only when you drink, or come with sweating, a racing heart, confusion, or hallucinations may be alcohol withdrawal. See a doctor, and don't stop heavy daily drinking suddenly without medical advice.
- Get emergency care for a seizure, confusion, hallucinations, high fever, or chest pain.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do my hands shake after drinking?**

After alcohol wears off, your nervous system rebounds into a slightly overexcited state, because your brain adjusted to alcohol's calming effect while you were drinking. Low blood sugar, stress hormones, poor sleep, dehydration, and caffeine can all add to it. In occasional drinkers this is a normal, short-lived part of a hangover. In people who drink heavily every day, the same process is much stronger and is called alcohol withdrawal.

**How do I get rid of the shakes after drinking?**

Eat something with carbohydrates and a bit of protein, sip water or an electrolyte drink if you've been sick, limit caffeine, rest, and try slow breathing to calm a racing heart. Avoid drinking more alcohol to steady your hands. Most hangover shakes ease within about 24 hours. If they don't, or if you drink heavily most days, see a doctor.

**How long do hangover shakes last?**

For most people, hangover shakes fade within a day as the rest of the hangover clears, often improving within a few hours of eating and rehydrating. A tremor that lasts several days after you stop drinking, or that gets worse instead of better, is more consistent with alcohol withdrawal and should be checked by a doctor.

**Are shakes after drinking a sign of alcohol withdrawal?**

They can be. A mild tremor after one heavy night is usually just a hangover. But shakes that show up most mornings, begin within hours of your last drink, ease when you drink again, or come with sweating, a fast heartbeat, agitation, or trouble sleeping suggest physical dependence. Withdrawal can be dangerous, so talk to a doctor before cutting back if you drink heavily every day.

**Is it safe to stop drinking if I get the shakes?**

If you're an occasional drinker who had one big night, yes. Simply not drinking again is fine. If you drink heavily every day and get shakes when you stop, quitting suddenly on your own can be risky, because severe withdrawal can cause seizures or delirium tremens. A doctor can assess you and make withdrawal much safer, often with medication. In the US, the SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-4357) can help you find treatment.

**Why does a drink stop the shakes?**

A drink temporarily replaces the alcohol your nervous system had adjusted to, so the rebound eases for a while. It only delays the problem. If alcohol is the thing that reliably stops your morning shakes, that's a sign your body may be becoming dependent on it, and it's worth talking to a doctor.

**When should I go to the ER for shaking after drinking?**

Go to the emergency room or call 911 if the shaking comes with a seizure, confusion, hallucinations, a very fast heart rate, chest pain, a high fever, or vomiting so severe you can't keep fluids down. People with diabetes should also get urgent help for shakiness with sweating and confusion that doesn't improve with sugar.

**Can low blood sugar cause shaking after drinking?**

Yes. While your liver processes alcohol, it makes less new glucose, so blood sugar can run low by morning, especially if you drank without eating. Low blood sugar triggers adrenaline, which causes shakiness, sweating, hunger, and a fast heartbeat. Eating some carbohydrates usually helps quickly. People with diabetes who use insulin or certain diabetes pills are at higher risk of dangerous lows after drinking.
